The Mahogany snapper (Lutjanus mahogoni) exhibits life-history traits typical of many tropical lutjanids, with reproductive investment closely tied to thermal conditions. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached approximately 14% [GSI = approximately 14%] when fish are maintained at a stable water temperature of 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C]. This index reflects the proportion of body mass devoted to ovarian tissue and is a reliable indicator of spawning readiness in captive broodstock. During annual field surveys along Caribbean reefs, gravid females are most frequently encountered during the summer months, suggesting that the observed GSI corresponds to the peak of the reproductive season. The initiation of vitellogenesis appears to be triggered by a combination of photoperiod and temperature cues, with the 25.8 °C thermal regime representing the approximate mean sea surface temperature during the breeding period. These reproductive parameters are essential for informing captive breeding programs and for constructing accurate population dynamics models for this commercially valuable species.

In terms of somatic growth, the Mahogany snapper attains a maximum or ultimate fork length of approximately 48 centimeters [Li = approximately 48 centimeters], a size that is typical for medium-bodied members of the genus Lutjanus. This asymptotic length is derived from length-frequency analyses and mark-recapture studies conducted across the species' range, where individuals rarely exceed this dimension even in protected areas with minimal fishing pressure. The corresponding computed ultimate wet weight for an adult of this length approaches 1584 grams [Wwi = 1584 grams], based on a length-weight relationship established from extensive sampling. This mass is substantial enough to confer a reproductive advantage, as larger females are capable of producing more numerous and larger batches of pelagic eggs. The growth trajectory to this terminal size is relatively rapid during the first few years of life, after which the rate of increase declines markedly as the fish approaches its physiological maximum. Comparisons with other Caribbean snappers indicate that this ultimate length is intermediate between the smaller lane snapper and the larger mutton snapper, reflecting a distinct ecological niche.

Female Mahogany snappers initiate reproductive maturation at a markedly smaller size than the ultimate adult dimensions, a pattern characteristic of many iteroparous reef fishes. The fork length at which fifty percent of females attain puberty has been estimated at 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters], a value that corresponds to roughly half the ultimate length. An individual reaching this size is predicted to have a wet weight of approximately 205 grams [Wwp = approximately 205 grams], derived from the same length-weight conversion used for the ultimate mass. This relatively early onset of reproductive maturity allows females to contribute to the population before they have fully completed somatic growth, a strategy that buffers against high adult mortality rates. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from fish collected across a size gradient confirms that vitellogenic oocytes first appear in specimens at or near the 24-centimeter (24 centimeters) [Lp = 24 centimeters] threshold. Such data are critical for establishing size limits in fisheries management, ensuring that a sufficient proportion of the spawning stock is protected before reaching harvestable size.

The early life history of Lutjanus mahogoni is characterized by an extremely small initial body mass, reflecting the production of pelagic eggs with minimal yolk reserves. Based on an egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters, a value reported for the congener Lutjanus stellatus, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams]. This minute mass is consistent with the energetics of batch spawning, where females release numerous small eggs to maximize larval dispersal and survival in a variable planktonic environment. Following a brief incubation period, the yolk-sac larva emerges at this diminutive size and must rapidly develop feeding structures to initiate exogenous nutrition before endogenous reserves are exhausted. The transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic feeding represents a critical mortality bottleneck, as larvae must encounter suitable prey items within a narrow window to avoid starvation. This low birth weight (0.00032 grams) [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] stands in stark contrast to the ultimate adult weight, underscoring the extraordinary magnitude of the ontogenetic size increase required to reach sexual maturity. Field data indicate that during each annual spawning season, females release approximately 5 viable eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5 viable eggs per spawning event] and complete roughly 2 to 3 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 2 to 3 spawning events per year].

Longevity records for the Mahogany snapper, compiled from otolith-based age estimation studies and tag-recapture programs, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6570 days [am = approximately 6570 days] at a mean annual water temperature of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C]. This considerable lifespan, equivalent to roughly eighteen years, positions this species as a relatively long-lived member of the Caribbean snapper assemblage, a trait that renders it vulnerable to overfishing if not managed cautiously. Individuals inhabiting cooler, deeper reef environments at the lower end of their thermal range may exhibit slightly extended longevities, though the 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C] figure represents the average temperature across most of the species distribution. The extended lifespan (6570 days) [am = 6570 days] allows for multiple reproductive opportunities across many breeding seasons, which is a hallmark of an iteroparous life-history strategy that buffers against occasional recruitment failures at a temperature of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C]. Furthermore, the combination of a long lifespan and a relatively moderate ultimate size of 48 centimeters [Li = 48 centimeters] suggests a slow-to-moderate pace of life, with substantial energetic investment in both somatic maintenance and repeated reproductive bouts, a pattern that is common among predatory reef fishes inhabiting stable tropical environments.
